cells.tense: You are here with your own sense of what is fair, and it is running clean.
cells.ask: Name one thing you feel owed and one thing you owe, out loud, to yourself, today.
cells.core:
You feel what fairness requires, and you can see the shape of a situation without getting caught in its details. You don't need a scoreboard. Someone takes more than their share and it registers, quietly, before you've argued with it.

This balance isn't a mood. It's a practice of checking the scale and finding it level. What feeds it next is the same motion — noticing what actually happened and letting that settle the account. Keep naming what you owe and what you're owed, one item at a time, and the scale stays readable. That is the work, and it is small enough to do today.

cells.tense: You will have already worked out what's fair before the moment even arrives.
cells.ask: Pick one relationship and let a single small debt go without mentioning it, ever.
cells.core:
You are running fairness ahead of the moment. Before something has actually happened, you have already worked out who owes what and what would make it even. The scene in your head is fully settled and the real one hasn't started. That bracing has a cost: you meet people already carrying the verdict.

Fairness that has to be computed in advance stops being a feel and becomes a calculation. The way back is not to feel less but to hold without forcing — to let the moment arrive with its own weight and let the scale tip on its own. Try releasing one small debt today, without balancing it. What usually happens is the exchange starts moving again.

cells.tense: You once knew what was fair on instinct, and that knowing is not speaking now.
cells.ask: Ask one person what they think is fair in a situation you're in, and repeat their answer back.
cells.core:
Something that used to be automatic isn't arriving. You watch a thing happen that would once have registered as wrong, and the feeling is late or absent. In its place there is a kind of blank reading, like the instrument is still there but not giving a number.

The move is not to force a moral feeling. It is to borrow someone else's read for a while — ask a person you trust what they see, out loud, and let their answer stand in for the one that isn't coming. Hearing fairness described by someone else is how the feel comes back on line. Then you can check it against your own sense, slowly.

cells.tense: You are already weighing right and wrong in ordinary moments, and calling it something else.
cells.ask: Catch one small judgment you make today and say, plainly, "that's a read I'm making."
cells.core:
You notice when a thing is off — a cut that was unfair, a share that came out uneven, a tone that landed wrong. It runs quietly, in the background, and shapes what you do and say. But you would not describe yourself as someone with a strong sense of justice. The judgment is operating without your name on it.

The recognition is already precise. What is missing is owning it openly. One honest claim out loud — that's a read, and it's yours — is enough to put your name back on the instrument. This is not about being more fair. It is about admitting the fairness is already yours.
cells.sheetLine: You already see what's fair. Say that it's yours.
